name: Boost.Asio
baseline: libuv (tcp-echo-server example from the libuv docs)
workload: TCP echo server on localhost, 1000 concurrent client sessions each sending 5000 messages (`time ./echo_server_client 1000 5000`), wall-clock seconds for the whole run; Asio C++20 coroutine echo server (one io_context built with BOOST_ASIO_CONCURRENCY_HINT_UNSAFE_IO, 1024-byte read buffer) against libuv's C tcp-echo-server doc example, plus Tokio, Go and Node.js servers.
claimed_speedup: Asio 29.5 s versus libuv 43.6 s for the same client run, about 1.48x less wall time (derived from page data); same table: Tokio 30.7 s, Go 35.6 s, Node.js 74.2 s. Benchmark author's own text: 'I expected Libuv to have similar performance to Asio and Tokio.'
hardware: Author's own machine, CPU model not stated; localhost loopback with 0.07 ms average latency per the benchmark doc
stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars (boostorg mirror); reference networking library for Boost and the C++ networking TS lineage
tradeoffs: Heavy template and header-only code with long compile times; proactor-style callbacks or coroutines with completion tokens have a steep learning curve; the benchmark's C++20 coroutine server needs a recent compiler.
caveats: Numbers come from the Boost.Redis repository's echo-server benchmark (written by the Boost.Redis author, not the Asio authors) and are not a dedicated Asio benchmark. They sit in the LaTeX source of the plot (benchmarks/benchmarks.tex, last edited 2022); the rendered doc page only shows a PNG that was not reachable here (boostorg.github.io blocked), so the .tex numbers were matched to the doc's prose (Go faster than Node.js and libuv; 1000 connections) rather than to the image. Compiler, flags and CPU are not stated, and the only machine detail is 'my machine'. The libuv baseline is the unmodified docs example, which mallocs a read buffer and a write request on every message, while the Asio server reuses one 1024-byte buffer per connection and runs with locking disabled (UNSAFE_IO hint), so it is an idiomatic-code comparison and not a tuned one. libuv is not the project's guessed baseline (libevent); no libevent row exists. Contrary data point in a third-party-style shootout: libhv's echo-servers benchmark (README on raw.githubusercontent.com/ithewei/libhv) measured asio at 132 MB/s versus libevent 157 MB/s and libuv 156 MB/s (4 threads, 1000 connections, 10 s), so Asio was slower there; the two benchmarks use different server code and clients.
found_via: seed-record pass (seed-list mining backfill): started from https://github.com/boostorg/asio; numbers found via WebSearch 'Boost.Asio vs libevent vs libuv echo server benchmark requests per second github', which surfaced the boostorg/redis echo-server benchmark
